Every Singapore vehicle plate ends with a letter worked out from the prefix and serial number. Enter yours, e.g. SCJ 2000, and get the last alphabet instantly.
VEHICLE REGISTRATION NUMBER CHECKSUM How the checksum is calculated The Land Transport Authority derives the last letter from the registration number so mistyped or misread plates can be detected:
Take the last two letters of the prefix and convert them to numbers (A = 1 … Z = 26). A one-letter prefix counts as 0 plus that letter. Write the serial number as four digits with leading zeros. Multiply the six figures by 9, 4, 5, 4, 3, 2 and add the results. Divide by 19; the remainder selects the letter from the table below. Remainder0123456789 LetterAZYXUTSRPM Remainder101112131415161718 LetterLKJHGEDCB Only 19 letters are needed, so F, I, N, O, Q, V and W never appear as the last letter of a Singapore plate.
Example: SCJ 2000. C = 3, J = 10, digits 2, 0, 0, 0. Then 3×9 + 10×4 + 2×5 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 77. 77 ÷ 19 leaves remainder 1, and position 1 in the table is Z. The full plate is SCJ 2000 Z.
Frequently asked questions Why does my plate have a letter at the end? It is a check character, like the last digit of an IC number. If a warden or camera system misreads one character of your plate, the checksum no longer adds up and the error is detected.
Which letters are never used as the last letter? F, I, N, O, Q, V and W. The remainder of the division is always 0 to 18, mapping to only 19 of the 26 letters.
Do government or event vehicles have a checksum letter? No. Special government vehicle plates and event vehicle plates skip the checksum letter entirely.
I ordered a custom 3D plate. Do the letters still need to follow this? The registration number is LTA assigned, The physical letters and numbers on your plate must meet OneMotoring size standards.
